title: Fix the Analogue Output Correction
statement:
This one is already written. It compiles without a murmur, the constants came
straight off a bench calibration, and it is wrong.

## The bug report

> Analogue output configured as 0-10V, tracking measured motor current. With
> the motor stopped -- current reading essentially zero -- the output sits at
> full-scale, close to 10V. It only "scales down" to a sensible,
> current-proportional reading once the motor starts drawing current.
> Expected behaviour is the opposite: near 0V at standstill, rising with
> current.

The editor starts with the code as it currently stands. Find the defect, fix
it, and leave the rest of the function alone.

## Your function

```
uint16_t scale_analogue_output(uint16_t raw);
```

`raw` is the pre-correction DAC value computed from a scaled current reading
elsewhere in the firmware -- a 12-bit quantity, `0..4095`, where `0` means the
sensor is reading nothing. Apply the bench-measured linear correction (a
gain, then an offset, both fixed-point -- the stored constants are the real
number times 1000, so the target never needs an FPU), clamp the result to the
DAC's `0..4095` range, and return it.

## What the tests will tell you

- `raw = 0`, the case from the bug report, is the one to look at first. Work
  out, by hand, what the buggy code actually returns for it -- not just that
  it's wrong, but what number it is and why the final `if` lets it through.
- Readings `0` through `3` all fail the same way; by `4` the fault has
  cleared. That boundary is not an accident of the test data -- something
  about the arithmetic genuinely changes there, and finding out what pins
  down the defect.
- `4095`, and a value past it, both come out the same before and after your
  fix. The clamp at the bottom of the function is not the problem. Noticing
  that narrows the search a lot.

## Watch out

- The fix is small, and it is not the clamp
  (`if (dw > AO_FULL_SCALE) { dw = AO_FULL_SCALE; }`). That comparison does
  exactly what it says. The trouble is what `dw` already equals by the time
  execution reaches it.
- `dw` is unsigned. Whatever your instinct says a subtraction "obviously"
  does when the mathematical result would be negative, check it against the
  type before you trust it.
- Wraparound on an unsigned type is well-defined C, not undefined behaviour --
  it is not a crash to go hunting for with a debugger. It is an ordinary,
  enormous number, silently produced, that the very next line's bounds check
  reads as "too big" rather than "went the wrong way."

tests.name: motor stopped: the reading the bug report describes
tests.description: raw is zero -- the current sensor reading nothing, motor at standstill. The buggy code returns 4095 (full-scale, ~10V) here instead of near-zero.

tests.name: the whole underflow band, back to back
tests.description: raw * 990 stays below the 3000 offset for 0..3, so the buggy subtraction underflows on all four of them; by raw = 4 it is clear of the band and both versions agree.

tests.name: near the top of the output's range
tests.description: The largest 12-bit input. Comfortably under the clamp -- the correction's gain is a shade under 1, so a correctly-corrected reading never legitimately reaches full scale in this design.

tests.name: a genuinely oversized value, clamped for real
tests.description: raw here is past the nominal 12-bit range (a couple of counts of rounding slop from the stage upstream, say). The corrected value genuinely comes out above 4095 and the clamp catches it correctly -- both the buggy and fixed code agree on this one, which is part of why the defect survived review: the clamp visibly works.
